questions.question: Why are distributed word embeddings preferred over one-hot representations?

options.text: They are smaller AND capture semantic similarity between words
They are easier to interpret by humans
They don't require training data
They are always sparse

questions.explanation: Dense embeddings are low-dimensional and place semantically similar words near each other in vector space.

questions.question: The Word2Vec skip-gram objective predicts:

options.text: The current word from surrounding context
Surrounding context words from the current word
The next sentence given the current one
Whether two documents are similar

questions.explanation: Skip-gram inverts CBOW: given a center word, predict its context words within a window.

questions.question: In scaled dot-product attention, why is the dot product divided by √dₖ?

options.text: To normalize the output to sum to 1
To prevent the softmax from saturating when dₖ is large
To enforce a positive-definite kernel
To speed up computation on GPU

questions.explanation: Large dₖ makes dot products grow in magnitude, pushing softmax into saturated regions with vanishing gradients. Scaling by √dₖ counteracts this.

questions.question: Subword tokenization (e.g. BPE) is useful because it:

options.text: Eliminates the need for embeddings
Handles rare and out-of-vocabulary words by composing them from subword units
Always produces fewer tokens than word tokenization
Works only for English

questions.explanation: BPE, WordPiece, and SentencePiece split rare words into known subunits, giving open-vocabulary coverage with a fixed vocabulary.

questions.question: What role do positional encodings play in a transformer?

options.text: They inject information about token order into an otherwise permutation-invariant architecture
They determine the learning rate
They replace the embedding layer
They are only used during inference

questions.explanation: Self-attention is permutation-invariant, so positional encodings (sinusoidal or learned) are added to embeddings to preserve sequence order information.

questions.question: In an LSTM cell, what is the role of the forget gate?

options.text: It decides which information from the previous cell state to discard by outputting values between 0 and 1 via a sigmoid activation
It forgets the current input so the model focuses on long-term memory only
It resets the hidden state to zero at the end of each sequence
It prevents the model from overfitting by randomly dropping connections

questions.explanation: The forget gate applies a sigmoid to the concatenation of the previous hidden state and current input, producing values in [0,1] that element-wise multiply the previous cell state. A value near 0 means 'forget this dimension', near 1 means 'keep it'. This selective forgetting is what allows LSTMs to learn long-range dependencies without gradient decay through the cell state highway.

questions.question: BERT's Masked Language Model (MLM) objective randomly masks 15% of input tokens. Of those masked tokens, 80% are replaced with [MASK], 10% with a random token, and 10% are kept unchanged. Why not replace all masked tokens with [MASK]?

options.text: To reduce the pretrain–finetune discrepancy: [MASK] never appears during fine-tuning, so the model must also learn to predict from non-masked contexts
To make training faster by reducing the number of masked positions
To implement dropout-like regularization at the token level
To ensure the vocabulary embedding for [MASK] does not dominate the representation space

questions.explanation: If all selected tokens were replaced with [MASK], the model would learn that it only needs to predict at [MASK] positions and would never see [MASK] during fine-tuning — creating a mismatch. The 80/10/10 split forces the model to maintain a good representation for every token (not just [MASK] positions), because any token might need to be predicted. The random-token replacement also prevents the model from relying on the identity of the input token as a shortcut.

questions.question: What is the key difference between Bahdanau (additive) attention and Luong (multiplicative) attention?

options.text: Bahdanau uses a learned feed-forward network to compute alignment scores, while Luong uses a dot product (or bilinear form) between decoder and encoder states
Bahdanau attention only works with GRU cells, while Luong attention only works with LSTMs
Luong attention uses the previous decoder state, while Bahdanau uses the current one
Bahdanau computes a single global attention vector, while Luong always uses local windowed attention

questions.explanation: Bahdanau attention computes alignment via a small neural network: score(s_i, h_j) = v^T tanh(W_1 s_i + W_2 h_j). Luong attention simplifies this to a dot product s_i^T h_j or a bilinear s_i^T W h_j, which is computationally cheaper. Note that distractor C reverses the actual timing: Bahdanau uses the previous decoder state (s_{i-1}), and Luong uses the current one (s_i). Luong also proposed local attention as one option, but is not restricted to it.

questions.question: Why do vanilla RNNs struggle with long-range dependencies?

options.text: Gradients are multiplied by the recurrent weight matrix at each time step, causing them to shrink exponentially when the largest eigenvalue is less than 1
RNNs can only process sequences shorter than 10 tokens
The softmax output saturates for long sequences
RNNs do not use backpropagation, so gradients cannot flow backward

questions.explanation: During backpropagation through time (BPTT), the gradient of the loss with respect to early inputs involves a product of Jacobians ∂h_i/∂h_{i-1}. When the largest eigenvalue of W_hh is < 1, this product shrinks exponentially with the number of time steps, making it impossible for the network to learn dependencies beyond ~10-20 steps. LSTMs address this with a cell state that provides an additive (rather than multiplicative) gradient path.

questions.question: How does GloVe differ from Word2Vec in its use of corpus statistics?

options.text: GloVe explicitly factorizes the log co-occurrence matrix with a weighted loss, while Word2Vec learns embeddings through local context prediction windows
GloVe uses character n-grams while Word2Vec uses whole words
GloVe trains on individual sentences while Word2Vec requires the entire corpus in memory
GloVe produces contextual embeddings while Word2Vec produces static ones

questions.explanation: GloVe (Global Vectors) explicitly constructs a global word-word co-occurrence matrix X and optimizes word vectors so that w_i · w_j + biases ≈ log(X_ij), weighted by f(X_ij) to downweight very frequent pairs. Word2Vec (Skip-gram/CBOW) instead uses local sliding windows to predict context words from target words (or vice versa). GloVe's key insight is that ratios of co-occurrence probabilities — not raw counts — encode meaning, which it captures through its matrix factorization objective. Distractor B describes FastText, not GloVe.

questions.question: In a Transformer with d_model = 512 and h = 8 attention heads, what is the dimensionality of each head's key, query, and value projections, and why is this design choice important?

options.text: d_k = d_v = 64 (512/8); this keeps the total computational cost comparable to single-head attention with full dimensionality while allowing each head to attend to different representational subspaces
d_k = d_v = 512; each head operates on the full dimension independently
d_k = d_v = 8; the number of heads equals the per-head dimension
d_k = d_v = 256; each head gets half the model dimension to reduce overfitting

questions.explanation: Multi-head attention splits the model dimension across heads: d_k = d_v = d_model / h = 512/8 = 64. Each head learns independent Q, K, V projections of size d_model × d_k, so the total parameter count for all heads (h × 3 × d_model × d_k = 8 × 3 × 512 × 64) is the same as a single attention with 3 × d_model × d_model projections. The key benefit is that different heads can specialize — some may track syntactic dependencies, others positional relationships, and others semantic similarity — without competing for the same representational capacity.

questions.question: How does FastText improve upon Word2Vec for handling out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words?

options.text: It represents each word as the sum of its character n-gram embeddings, so unseen words can be composed from known subword pieces
It uses a larger vocabulary that includes all possible words in all languages
It assigns a special [UNK] embedding trained on all rare words collectively
It falls back to character-level RNN encoding for any word not in the vocabulary

questions.explanation: FastText (Bojanowski et al., 2017) extends Skip-gram by representing each word as a bag of character n-grams (e.g., 'where' → '<wh', 'whe', 'her', 'ere', 're>'). The word embedding is the sum of its n-gram embeddings. For OOV words, the same decomposition produces a meaningful vector from known n-grams, unlike Word2Vec which has no representation at all for unseen words. Distractor B is impossible (infinite vocabulary), C collapses all rare words to one vector (losing semantics), and D describes a different architecture entirely.

questions.question: What is the key architectural insight of T5 (Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer) that distinguishes it from BERT and GPT?

options.text: T5 frames every NLP task — classification, translation, summarization, Q&A — as a text-to-text problem with task-specific prefixes, using a single encoder-decoder architecture for all tasks
T5 uses a bidirectional encoder like BERT but generates output tokens autoregressively, making it strictly superior to both BERT and GPT on all benchmarks
T5 eliminates positional encodings entirely, relying on causal masking alone to encode sequence order
T5 pretrains with a standard next-token prediction objective identical to GPT, but at much larger scale

questions.explanation: T5 (Raffel et al., 2020) unifies all NLP tasks into a single sequence-to-sequence format: the input is 'task prefix: input text' and the output is always text. For example, classification becomes 'classify: The movie was great' → 'positive'; translation becomes 'translate English to German: Hello' → 'Hallo'. This text-to-text framework means the same model, loss function, and hyperparameters work for every task. T5 does use an encoder-decoder architecture (distractor B is partially right but wrong to claim strict superiority), it uses relative positional encodings (not none — distractor C), and it uses a span-corruption denoising objective (not GPT-style next-token — distractor D).
